That when this house adjourns on Friday, March 2, 1956, it stand adjourned until Monday, March 5, 1956, at 3.30 o'clock in the afternoon.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF TRADE AGREEMENT WITH SOVIET UNION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF TRADE AGREEMENT WITH SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to announce the conclusion of a trade agreement with the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. The text of this agreement is being tabled for the information of hon. members. If the house agrees, I suggest that the text be printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings.
My colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), opened the way for this agreement during his visit to the U.S.S.R. last October. At that time it was agreed in exploratory talks that negotiations should take place in Ottawa. A delegation
from the U.S.S.R. arrived here four weeks ago, and the negotiations have been in progress since then.
The agreement which has been reached is set forth in five documents.
The first of these documents makes provision for the exchange of most-favourednation treatment along lines similar to existing agreements with various other countries. It includes other provisions having to do with the conduct of trade between the two countries. It recognizes that either government may apply prohibitions or restrictions of any kind for the protection of its essential security interests. Our strategic export controls are therefore not affected. This agreement provides in addition on a reciprocal basis for the non-discriminatory treatment of merchant ships while in port. On the Canadian side, the effect of this latter provision is simply to confirm the treatment which in fact has been available all along to ships of U.S.S.R. registry.
This agreement is to continue in force for a period of three years; agreement of both countries is required for any extension. It was signed on February 29 by accredited representatives of both governments and is now in force provisionally. By its terms, it is subject to ratification within 90 days from the date of signature and within this time opportunity will be provided for a debate in parliament. A resolution of approval will be introduced for this purpose.
The second document is a letter from the Canadian government reserving the right to establish values for ordinary and special import duty on any Russian product that might enter Canada in such increased quantities as to cause serious injury to domestic producers. In determining such values, the prices of similar goods imported into Canada from third countries are to be taken into account. This procedure is intended to deal with situations which might be created if Russian goods were to be sold in Canada at very low prices, even if they are not proven to be lower than their domestic values in the U.S.S.R.
The third document is a letter from the government of the U.S.S.R. acknowledging the Canadian letter on customs valuation.

Trade Agreement with Russia
The fourth of the five documents forming the agreement is a letter by which the government of the U.S.S.R. guarantees to purchase and take delivery from Canada, during the three years of the agreement, a total of between 1,200,000 and 1,500,000 tons of wheat, in annual lots of between 400,000 and 500,000 tons. The exact amounts to be purchased in the second and third years, within these annual amounts, will be determined by the government of the U.S.S.R., taking into account the volume of Soviet goods sold to Canada. The total over the three years, however, will amount to not less than 1,200,000 tons and the amount in any individual year to not less than 400,000 tons. The Russian purchases of wheat are to be made at the prices and on the terms at which the Canadian wheat board is making sales to its major customers at such times as the Soviet purchases take place.
The fifth document is a letter from the Canadian government, acknowledging the letter from the government of the U.S.S.R. on wheat.

1.	Have cleaners, messmen, fumacemen and employees in similar categories working on Royal Canadian Air Force stations across Canada yet been put on the five day week?
2.	If not, at what stations has the five day week not yet been put into effect for such employees?
3.	Is consideration being given to putting all such employees, on all Royal Canadian Air Force stations in Canada, on the five day week? If so, when will this take place?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to part 1 of this question is that when the government implemented the five day week for operating staffs, certain categories of employees were excluded. Among the excluded categories are staffs engaged in providing food and housekeeping service to civil servants, military personnel, and transient guests. Employees of the R.C.A.F. in the classification messmen have, accordingly, not been placed on the five day week. Some R.C.A.F. employees in the classification of cleaner and helper provide service to living accommodation.
Because it is considered inadvisable to have employees in the same classification at the same location working varying work weeks, the standard 44-hour work week, with one minor exception, has been retained for cleaners and helpers employed by the R.C.A.F. Heating staffs employed by the R.C.A.F. work a standard five day 40-hour week at locations designated by the government, in accordance with the announced policy. In some instances, it has not yet been possible to obtain sufficient qualified staff to implement fully the five day week for heating staffs. Where this is the case, overtime compensation is given for hours worked in excess of 40 per week.
The answer to part 2 of the question is that the five day week is not in effect for such employees at the following R.C.A.F. locations: Goose Bay, Newfoundland; Debert and Greenwood, Nova Scotia; Lac St. Denis, Mont Apica, Parent, Senneterre, Moisie, St. Sylvestre and Rimouski, province of Quebec; Edgar, Foymount, Angus, Fingal, Collins Bay and Mountain View, Ontario; Gimli and Macdonald, Manitoba; Claresholm, Penhold and Cold Lake, Alberta; Fort Nelson, British Columbia; and White Horse, Snag, Teslin, Smith River, Aishihik, Watson Lake in the Yukon Territory.
As to part 3, a fairly full statement on policy in respect of these categories of

employment was given to the house by the then minister of finance, Mr. Abbott, on February 16, 1954, as appears at page 2122 of Hansard of that year. Government policy on the hours of work for federal employees is periodically reviewed and when changes are to be made they will be made known at that time.

Inquiries of the Ministry the Minister of Justice. speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had a chance to read the article in question, and my comment would be that since confederation the responsibility for the custody of a prisoner sentenced to death and the responsibility for the actual carrying out of the death sentence has been that of the provinces. During this long period of time they never questioned this responsibility and have carried it out.
It seems to me that if any change in this responsibility were to be considered at all it should not be considered until we shall have received the report of the parliamentary committee on capital and corporal punishment and lotteries, the preparation of which is shortly to be under way. Until we shall have received that report we should not consider requests of this nature, and that is the position I took in the letter of reply which I wrote to Hon. Mr. Sturdy.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question? In view of the fact that the Saskatchewan government has turned its jails into corrective institutions where young men are incarcerated, does the minister think some arrangement could be made between the provinces and his department so that executions may be removed from these corrective institutions to places where more hardened criminals are incarcerated if we are going to continue capital punishment at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, any arrangements that we make with any one province, I think we would have to be prepared to provide for others. No one has suggested until the present time that the manner in which the province carries out death sentences is other than a provincial responsibility. I would be quite open to suggestions as to any means by which we might be of help to the carrying out of death sentences by this province. But we could not consider assuming this responsibility ourselves or even consider a consideration of assuming it until we receive the report of this committee. Otherwise we would be anticipating the report of the committee in a manner which would be most inappropriate.

speechtext:
I would like to give the further information promised yesterday to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne).
The regional office for the Atlantic provinces is at Moncton. All claims from the two offices of Campbellton and Edmundston, as from others, have to pass through the regional office for processing and then return to the local offices for payment. Therefore the number of claims actually under process at the regional office varies from day to day.
Only by physical count is it possible to get a picture of the status of the claims flowing through the regional office on any given day. In view of yesterday's question, I asked the commission if they would conduct a detailed count and report on the status of all claims at the Moncton regional office, originating from the local offices of Campbellton and Edmundston, as at the close of business yesterday.
Also the points at issue are not only the number of claims but rather the question of undue delay or the length of time that they have been under process since the date the claims were filed at the local office.
With that explanation, I now give the results of last night's work at Moncton regional office. A physical count of all claims originating in the above two offices and pending at the Moncton regional office was made last evening, February 28. The following is the breakdown:
Campbellton, N.B., office:	168 regular
claims. Of the 168 regular claims, 118 are less than one week old. I interject here that by "old" I mean the length of time since the claim was first filed at the local office. 36 are less than two weeks old; 8 are less than three weeks old; 6 are three weeks old or more.
Edmundston, N.B., office: 128 regular claims. Of the 128 regular claims, 91 are less than a week old; 27 are less than two weeks old; 7 are less than three weeks old; 3 are three weeks old or more.
Delays in regular claims are for various reasons, some beyond the commission's -control, such as: (1) Awaiting credits for contributions payable in respect of service in the armed forces; (2) insurance books lost or mislaid by claimants, requiring reference
Inquiries of the Ministry to previous employers for particulars of contributions; (3) awaiting transfer of contribution records from other regions in respect of claimants who worked in other than the Atlantic region and have since moved there.
The figures would not be complete without this reference. It will be recalled that in my statement in the house on 25th January 1 said there would be some delay in the computation of certain claims to be reconsidered under the reinterpretation of 119 (b) of the act, because of the heavy loads that the offices would have to encounter.
Therefore, I would like also to report on those that are at the regional office, Moncton, in this category, as of last night.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent (Quebec East):
That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may be referred to it and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.

Mr. Speaker, last night just prior to the adjournment, following your second last intervention, as recorded on page 1655 of Hansard, I commented to you in reference to the earlier intervention of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) that the hon. member did not put a question. Then Hansard records that an hon. member said, "Yes, he did."
I should like to make this comment. It is quite true that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine asked a question and it is indeed true that he asked three questions. I accepted his questions and endeavoured to answer them. But what I was referring to at that time was the fact that after I had answered his three questions he then insisted on getting up and making a statement. That was what I was referring to in this statement that I made, which another hon. member has apparently thought was alluding to the earlier questions of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine.
Sir, prior to the intervention of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) I was, as Hansard records at the bottom of the page 1654, the first column, making this singularly unprovocative remark:
I made mention of the way the committee on estimates functions at Westminster. The committee there decides what estimates-
Then there is a dash and then the intervention of the hon. gentleman began. I did not return to the thread of my comment. I wish to deal with the practice at Westminster in reference to the selection of work on the part of the committee on estimates. The committee on estimates at Westminster decides what work that committee will take in hand in review of estimates. I am informed that in the first instance they usually refer that subject to a subcommittee of the main committee. I suppose in our practice here we would call it the steering committee. That subcommittee consists of the chairman, the chairmen of all five subcommittees and also two or three senior members of the committee on estimates. The opposition, through their representatives on that subcommittee or steering committee, has full scope in the choice of the estimates to be examined.

The recommendations of the subcommittee or steering committee are then submitted to the whole committee and a decision is taken there in the light of the recommendations of the subcommittee. So you will see there is no attempt on the part of the government to select, before the committee even meets or is set up, the work that the committee is to undertake. The committee makes its own decision as to what estimates it is to consider. The whole estimates of a department may be referred to one of the five subcommittees for examination or the estimates of several departments, but frequently only certain items of the estimates of one or more departments under which money is provided for certain purposes are referred. The complete freedom of the estimates committee to select the work that it is to take up is emphasized at every stage of the procedure.
We have been told that this is the continuation of an experiment. We had one year's experience with the experiment. I suggest that if the experiment is to continue we ought to make it a useful experiment. Last year we experimented with a system under which the opposition was given no voice whatever in the selection of the departments. The government itself, before the committee was permitted to function, made the selection of the departments. If we are going to experiment further, then let us extend the scope of the experiment. Let us experiment this year with a committee that has a free hand to select its own business in review of the estimates.
Having experimented last year with a committee that was hamstrung and fettered, let us experiment this year with an unfettered committee and derive the benefit of the experience from it. I propose therefore to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by deleting therefrom the words "as may be referred to it" and substituting therefor the following: "as may seem fit to the committee."
I point out to the house that if the amendment is adopted it will bring the powers and procedures of the committee in this regard completely into line with the well established practice at Westminster, a practice that has now been in effect for 44 years and is working to the satisfaction of all political parties there.
Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that there was a time when the practice at Westminster with regard to the committee on estimates was apparently approved by the government here. As found at page 937 of
Committee on Estimates Hansard for February 8, 1955, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), in introducing the resolution, said this:
Of course, in the years since the world war there has been repeated discussion on the subject and in each of the committees on procedure which have been set up we have had extensive talks as to the method by which to bring about a better way of dealing with the estimates.
Then, note these words:
If hon. members are interested, they would have noticed that the 1947 committee recommended that we adopt in general terms the system obtaining in the United Kingdom.
I take it that the Minister of Finance would not have made that observation on the report of the 1947 committee of this house on procedure were he not putting that reference forward with approval. I say to all members of the house that if they wish to pay attention to the recommendation of the 1947 committee of this house on procedure they will proceed to bring the powers and procedures of the proposed committee on estimates into line with those prevailing at Westminster. They can do that in this respect by adopting the present amendment. If they do not adopt the present amendment they are simply proposing to continue a fettered and hamstrung committee. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move the amendment.

I was giving a paraphrase. I was not reading directly. I was giving a paraphrase from a source from which I have had full instructions on the procedure prevailing at Westminster. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, if you wish, that it is from an hon. member of that house of long experience.

Mr. Speaker, as one who was a member of the committee on estimates last year from the beginning and who was present at almost all hearings, and consequently as one of those who had to listen to the same diatribe that we have had to listen to from the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), I think I should ask the indulgence of the house for a few minutes today. As we all
1670	HOUSE OF
Committee on Estimates know, when the committee was set up last year the official opposition put up a barrage of technical amendments and adopted all kinds of tactics to delay the proceedings of the committee and to prevent the committee from getting to work on the estimates of the departments.
Nonsense.
The hon. member for Eglinton is not in a position to speak on that particular point because, although he was a member originally, he remained a member for a very short while.
It is all on record.

But I admit that his colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, certainly tried to emulate him in this respect. As every member who was on the committee for any length of time knows, as soon as the hon. member for Kamloops was taken off the committee the committee got to work and from that day on we did very useful work.
Whitewashing the government.

The record speaks for itself. Anybody can look at the record. If you open Hansard for last year you will find that members from all quarters of the house, members of the official opposition as well as members of the C.C.F. and Social Credit groups and members on the government side, agreed that the committee had served a very useful purpose last year. Some did have certain qualifications. That is understandable coming from the opposition, but after some weeks of sitting, after we actually got down to work on the estimates, it is apparent from the record that the committee served a very useful purpose to the house and to the members themselves.
The only trouble with the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Eglinton is that when they came to the committee they attempted to do everything else but consider the estimates. This committee is a committee on estimates. The purpose of the committee is to consider the estimates of the department which is referred to the committee. The attempt made from the very beginning was to try to do something altogether outside of that jurisdiction. Then even when the time came to consider the estimates, the effort of the hon. member for Kamloops was to bring someone from outside to do the questioning for him.
To get a witness before the committee.

We all know the hon. member for Kamloops. He is an intelligent gentleman. He is a lawyer and even a Rhodes scholar. IMr. Jutras.]

Yesterday he complained that he could not come to grips with the estimates. If he had applied himself in any way to coming to grips with the estimates, I am sure that he could have done so without any difficulty. However, as I say, he was in a frame of mind where he was so imbued with the idea of having somebody from outside or of doing something else apart from considering the estimates that, as he put it, he found it extremely frustrating indeed to be on that committee. I just want to remind him that if he was frustrated, he has no idea how annoyed the rest of the members of the committee were when we had to put up with these delaying tactics in sitting after sitting of the committee.
In the discussion yesterday and today the point made by both hon. members of the official opposition is twofold, as I understand it. First of all, they complain of the inability to send for persons, papers and records. I see that Mr. Speaker is looking at me. We had an amendment with respect to that matter and I am prevented from referring to it. I will certainly refrain from doing so, Mr. Speaker, although I should very much like to refer to it.
We now come to the next point. The next point raised by both hon. gentlemen-and it was raised today by the hon. member for Eglinton who indeed moves an amendment to that effect-is this. If I may I should like to read from the speech of the hon. member for Kamloops. As reported at pages 1639 of Hansard he said:
The second obvious limitation is that the committee will have before it for consideration only such estimates as the government by the control of its majority in the house may refer to it.
That in effect is the complaint of the hon. member for Eglinton, if I understood him correctly. Although I have not the wording of the amendment before me, the amendment is in effect trying to correct that situation. What is the complaint in this regard? The complaint of the opposition is that the matter of referring the departments to the committee is left to parliament. That is what it is. He says that it has for consideration "only such estimates as the government by the control of its large majority in the house may refer to it". In other words-and this is strange indeed-here is the official opposition complaining because it is left within the authority of parliament to decide what will come to the committee. They are arguing and then moving an amendment with a view to taking this authority out of parliament and placing it in a committee of the house. That suggestion seems strange to me, coming from the official opposition.
Why do you not be realistic about it?

It is not a question of being
realistic. All matters are referred to the committee by parliament, not by the government. Now the complaint is that parliament is dominated by the government members. Of course that is so and it always will be the situation no matter who is in power. The majority in parliament decides but it is parliament that decides. It is parliament that decides what departments will come before the committee. Now we have this odd situation of finding the official opposition complaining that this authority should be removed from parliament because parliament is not competent to decide what departments should go before the committee.

How ridiculous can you
become?

That is a complete reversal of the stand of the opposition, if I may say so.
Extensive reference has been made to the United Kingdom committee on estimates. The one thing-and it is a most important thing- that all hon. members who referred to it failed to point out is that in the United Kingdom, as we know, the estimates have become so extensive, voluminous and large that members of parliament have given up the task of trying to study every one of the estimates in their parliament. As a compromise they have this estimates committee and all they attempt to do is to make a spot check, so to speak, on the estimates. Hence of necessity they are obliged to take certain items or certain departments in order to make a study of those particular items. But there is never any attempt to go through all the estimates. Here in this country we are still at the stage where the amount of our estimates and the number of our estimates are such that it is still physically possible for parliament and for a committee to make a detailed study of every item of our estimates. That is what we were doing last year with all the departments which came before our committee. We made an extensive and detailed study of every department that came before us.
I did not hear the opposition suggest that we should adopt the United Kingdom practice. I do not think we have yet reached that stage. I do not say that we may not reach it before very long. I recall, for instance, that a few years ago we streamlined our estimates. We reduced the number of our estimates because they were getting fairly bulky and difficult to run through. But today I suggest that it is practical yet for the committee to make a complete study of the estimates. I suggest
Committee on Estimates that the example of the United Kingdom type of committee which is set up for a different purpose altogether is not a fair comparison and does not apply to this country.
Reference was made to the United States committee or to their standing committees in congress.
No. No reference was made to that matter.
Yes, there was. It was not made by you. Some other members made reference to it. Of course over there in the United States there is a different set-up altogether.
There was not any reference at all to it in this debate.
Yes. I recall some reference to it.
A year ago; not in this debate.
If I wish to make reference to it, I am entitled to do so. There is nothing to prevent me from doing it.
It is a red herring.

Let me say this to the hon. member. There are many people in this country-and I have run across the situation on many occasions-and many members in the opposition who are confused on many occasions. They see what goes on in Washington. They see how the system operates over there. Then we here in this country get requests for more or less getting the same thing done in Canada. They of course forget that we operate under quite different systems of government.
Shortly before the opening of this session it was my privilege to visit one of the standing committees of congress. As a matter of fact, I was invited to sit around the table with the members of the committee for part of a sitting and I was able to observe closely how their committee was operated. It is not for me to judge their method of procedure, but I certainly came out convinced that it could not be applied or followed with the system of government that we have. As I say, their system of government is entirely different from ours and their procedure does not apply here.
After all, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Kamloops or any other hon. member of the opposition says that with this type of committee he has been unable to come to grips with the problem in the estimates committee, I suggest that if he has been unable to do so it is simply because he has not applied himself to the task. Towards the end of the session particularly, everybody expressed the feeling that a good job had been done by the committee. At no time did the ministers refuse to answer any questions
1672	HOUSE OF
Committee on Estimates that were asked by either opposition or government members. At no time did the ministers or anyone else refuse to produce officials of the department for questioning by the committee. We had all the help of the department and all the officials who were asked to be present came. All the information was laid before the members. As some hon. members pointed out, we not only got a lot of information but I am sure all members learned a great deal about the various departments. I am sure the committee could function in the same way this year.
In conclusion, I should like to read one sentence that was uttered by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) in the committee last year. We had completed an examination of the first department to come before the estimates committee, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Everybody was commenting on the success of the committee up to that stage. Speaking for the opposition, the hon. member for St. Paul's said:
I should also like to put myself and my associates on record in expressing our appreciation of the assistance which has been given to this committee,-
He was referring to the officials who had appeared before the committee. He continues: -and I would like also to say that I hope Mr. Thatcher has recovered from his deep pessimism about the prospects of this committee.
I commend those words to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher).

I have listened to this debate during this session and the last session with some interest. I feel that a lot of the discussion is irrelevant. If one reads the resolution, one finds it is wide open. It merely asks us to set up a committee to which estimates can be referred from time to time. There is not anything in the motion itself that refers to any particular department.
We were told on February 9 what they were going to be.

It has been suggested that there are certain departments that would be referred, and it is with that point I wish to quarrel for a few minutes. I think that setting up a committee with the end in view as expressed by the official opposition that ultimately all estimates should get a working over by that committee, would mean the abdication of parliament. It is the duty of this parliament, in committee of the whole, to examine the estimates and not send 30 men from the house to go out and examine them without the remainder of the house knowing [Mr. Jutras.l

anything about the discussion. It certainly is not giving the other members of the house much chance to decide whether the money voted is legitimate or otherwise.
Another tendency this committee has, Mr. Speaker, is to make the rest of the members lazy. If you appoint two or three members from each group in the house to examine the estimates, it is their responsibility and the rest of the members are not going to look at the estimates. They are going to depend on their members on the committee. Another thing, at the end of the session when the estimates are being considered you will often find that the members on the committee, who you expected would be discussing those estimates are not here. Other members in the group did not look at the estimates because they felt that was the responsibility of the member appointed to the committee.
In my opinion, and it is my own opinion, the sending of the estimates of the departments of labour, health and welfare and the other two departments is unnecessary. I feel it is not very much trouble to examine the estimates of a department of government that is spending the money within the country. I do not think any committee will take the estimates of any department in which the money is spent in the country and change the estimates by one cent. If you look at the items in the estimates of the department that are to be sent to the committee, you will find every one of them is a fixed responsibility. The amount changes from time to time, but not very much. I believe the department officials could justify any of those expenditures. The fact of the matter is that in labour, health and welfare and post office we are asking for increased expenditures all the time, not reductions.
I think if each group in the house did what this group has been doing we would not have much trouble examining estimates. Before the estimates are brought down each member of this group is told he will be responsible for a certain department. I am told, "Your departmental estimates will be labour." It is my responsibility to take the labour department estimates and go over them item by item. If I think there is something wrong in some section I can pick up the telephone and get the information. If I do not like what I am told I can criticize the item here when the Department of Labour estimates are before the committee of the whole. I am in a position to do that because this group has given me that responsibility. One member of this group is responsible for going over the estimates of one particular department.

I do agree with the appointment of the committee, and for this reason. In the estimates this year $1,775 million have been allocated to the Department of National Defence; $15 million to defence production and $7 million to civil defence. All these defence expenditures amount to about 39-20 per cent of the total tax dollar. If there are any departments in which there could be waste and extravagance or duplication in money spent outside of the country, where it is difficult for any member of this house to make an examination of the justification of the amounts spent, it is in those departments. I think those departments should be examined by a committee. I do not think it should be a committee appointed merely to work over the estimates. As I have said for a good many years, when you have one minister responsible for three defence departments, the navy, army and air force-even although he has excellent deputies-when you are spending money on NATO all over the world; when you have money going into civil defence, a new type of organization about which we know little, then I think someone should take a look at these expenditures. Defence production is another one. Purchases are made for the defence department. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) is not in any position to report to this house with any degree of accuracy as to whether the money is being used judiciously or otherwise.
If we are to set up a committee, then it should be a continuing committee. The spending that we should be examining is the spending of the departments that I have mentioned. They are not fixed responsibilities. A great deal of money is going into that particular organization, and if a committee were appointed by this house, and if the members of that committee were picked carefully, they would sit there and work conscientiously. If that committee had the right, as suggested by the amendment just proposed, to call in the heads of different departments to give an account of their stewardship, the committee would be a brake on defence spending. The fact that they could be called in would place the men who are spending that money in the position where they would take another look at every item. They would do that if they were answerable to a committee of this house.
I imagine that expenditures on defence are going to be with us as long as most of us will live. These expenditures are growing all the time, and they will continue to grow and become greater. If we want a committee, then I suggest to hon. members that we are wasting time by putting before that committee for examination estimates that are fixed responsibilities. I do not think they get as 67509-106
Committee on Estimates good an examination in that way as they would get if they were taken up in the house and worked over in the ordinary way. It would require little change. A great deal of value would be derived from setting up a continuing committee whose responsibility it would be to consider the various defence departments. I have just suggested civil defence, defence production and the general national defence departments.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion on this committee. I find myself at a loss to agree entirely with the arguments adduced, but I must admit that many points have been thought-provoking. I think they are real. If we had some medium by which we could take the good points of these arguments and crystallize them into action, then we would be serving a more useful function.
There has been discussion as to the method by which the estimates should be presented for perusal. I think it is impossible for any estimates committee to deal with them intelligently at any one session. It might be worthy of consideration to take them in order of importance and perhaps rotate them so that there would be enough estimates presented to occupy the full time of the committee authorized to deal with them. I am inclined to believe, from what I saw as a member of that committee, that nothing would be presented that would cause the government any worry if they agreed to the request that the committee be given the right to call in anyone to enlighten them on the job they have to do. I do not think it necessarily means that with respect to every estimate that comes up you would be calling in scores of people from the outside. I do not think that is necessary at all. But if on the discussion of the estimates a reasonable doubt should arise, and we should have a little further information, then we should have the right to call for that information. I think that is conducive to good business. I would be the last one in the world to subscribe to that suggestion if I thought it was going to become a medium for political manoeuvring, where people were jockeying for political aggrandizement. I do not think that should be done at all.
There is another thing that I feel is not conducive to good business, and that is to have ministers sitting in as members of the committee. I have the highest regard for all of the hon. gentlemen, but I do not think I can reconcile that with my own good judgment. I do not think they should sit in as judge and jury both, and that is really what they are doing. It would be better in many

Committee on Estimates ways to have them sit there in their true capacity and not be identified as a member of the committee.
At this point I should like to pay tribute to the ministers for the frankness with which they answered all the questions that were put to them. I should like to pay a tribute to those of their staffs who were so efficient and so ready with their answers to the problems that were perplexing members of the committee at that time. That is all to the good. They are to be highly commended; but I think we should consider the advisability of having the minister sit in the committee in the capacity of both judge and jury.
I heard certain statements made. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) commented on the amount of valuable time that was wasted through debating whether or not we should be privileged to call in witnesses. If it were recognized that they would be available if necessary-and it would be necessary only rarely-then it would relieve the tension and give us perhaps a greater opportunity more intelligently to deal with the business in hand.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us has been carefully explained by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). The purpose of the amendment is clear. It would have as its effect an arrangement similar to that which has proved so satisfactory at Westminster where this practice was adopted. I regret very much that in regard to a matter so important to this house we should have no statement from the government on the motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister. We are still waiting to hear from the Prime Minister any reason why the reasonable requests made on an earlier motion, and now before the house on this motion, cannot be considered by the government. The only statements that have been made, other than the very numerous interjections from a seated position, are the statements made on February 9 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), in which he made no attempt to explain why the government was not following the very satisfactory practice adopted at Westminster, and the statements we have just heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras).
If anything favourable can be said about the speech of the hon. member for Provencher it is that it did at least attempt to deal with some aspects of the discussion now before us. The Minister of Finance, in a few words on February 9, as reported at page 1041 of Hansard of this session, simply informed the house that we were not going to
[Mr. Yulll.l
have this procedure that has proved satisfactory elsewhere. He also gave certain bald information, without explanation, as to why that was being done. For that reason, we are brought up to the statement of the hon. member for Provencher today, because it becomes necessary to deal with one or two statements he made, in view of the fact that we have no other statements to deal with in regard to this subject. The hon. member for Provencher told us today, in what sounded like an attempt to make an authoritative statement, "It is for parliament to decide what departments will go before the committee." Mr. Speaker, nothing could better illustrate how important it would be that this subject be dealt with under the established procedure, because the hon. member for Provencher obviously does not know anything about it.
The hon. member for Provencher is obviously unaware that on February 9 the Minister of Finance stated that two months ago, that was two months before February 9, the decision had been made. These are his words as found at page 1042 of Hansard:
We had considered what estimates we might refer to the committee this year. We did that some two months ago and decided to refer to the committee the estimates of the Department of Labour, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of National Revenue and the Post Office Department.
Since the only statement that has even pretended to give anything in the way of an explanation has been made by the hon. member for Provencher, I think I should put on the record a letter I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the reply I received. It will be quite clear from that, if there is any uncertainty in the mind of any hon. member, that parliament has not been asked to decide and that this decision was made in December and was made by the government. When the Minister of Finance says, "We decided" he means the government and not parliament. Parliament was not sitting in December; hon. members know that parliament met on January 10.
On January 27 I wrote the following letter to the Prime Minister:
The Rt. Hon. Louis St. Laurent. P.C., Q.C., M.F., Prime Minister of Canada,
House of Commons.
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Prime Minister:
In view of the fact that a motion stands in your name on the Order Paper to set up a committee to deal with estimates, I thought I should indicate to you the departmental estimates which we would prefer to have considered.

In the following order, we would like to have the committee consider the estimates of these departments:
Defence
Trade and Commerce
Justice
Fisheries.
I would hope that it might be decided this year that the committee will have power to call witnesses and obtain the production of papers and records. Naturally this power would be subject to review by the committee in any case where security might be involved. I do urge, however, that subject to this reservation, provision be made that the committee have this power.
Yours sincerely,
The letter is signed by me.
In reply I received the following letter dated February 2:
The Honourable George Drew, P.C., Q.C., LL.D., Leader of the Opposition,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Drew:
May I thank you for your letter of January 27 with respect to the business of the estimates committee.
Last December we considered this question and decided that we would refer to the committee the estimates of the Departments of National Revenue, Labour, Health and Welfare and Post Office, and these departments have been making suitable arrangements in the meantime. Under the circumstances I do not think it would be desirable to change these plans.
With respect to your request that the committee have power to call witnesses and require the production of papers and records, may I point out that the Minister of Finance, in moving the setting up of this committee last session, made it clear that as this was an innovation it was desirable, in the experimental period, to keep the work of the committee as close as possible to the practice and procedure in the committee of supply. 1 think you will agree we are still in the experimental period, and we would prefer to continue the experiment on the basis begun last year.
Yours sincerely.
The letter is signed by the Prime Minister.
It is quite clear that the decision was made in December and that no choice has been left to parliament to make any decision in this respect.
The suggestion has been made, by the only spokeman from the government side who has even pretended to deal with this subject, that the opposition is complaining that parliament must decide what will be done. That statement is pure unadulterated nonsense. Parliament is not being asked to decide. Where is there anything before this house that places parliament in the position to make any requests? What we are complaining about is that parliament has no chance to decide and we by this resolution are giving parliament a chance to actually have some authority. We are proposing a method that would be consistent with the procedure followed in the jurisdiction upon which this practice is based. I would point 67509-106i
Committee on Estimates out, however, that we need not go to Westminster to find reasons why there should be the right to call witnesses and also to call for the production of papers and documents. Every standing committee of this house has that authority now. Under the rules of this house every standing committee has the right and power to call for the attendance of witnesses and the production of papers and documents. We are not suggesting some strange innovation.
May I say that the only place from which any suggestion has come that we should make a comparison with the procedure in the United States is from the hon. member for Provencher. It would appear that he had gone to Washington to see if there was anything there which we might follow, for he tells us of his experience following the activities of that committee. Certainly we are not suggesting the adoption of a policy of that kind. We are suggesting the application of a procedure already incorporated in our rules in regard to standing committees. All that would be necessary to make this possible now would be for the government to decide that this committee will become a standing committee, and I make that proposal now, that this committee be a standing committee.
It has already been suggested here that this committee meet regularly. We want it to meet regularly. Let us have it a standing committee and then automatically it would have the right to call witnesses and to call for the production of papers and documents. As it is, this committee is nothing but a pious pretence. When the hon. member for Provencher said that they all came out satisfied with what had been done, he meant that the Liberals all came out satisfied that they had suppressed any opportunity of really getting at the facts that would have been available if witnesses had been called. That was the satisfaction they felt.
We listened this afternoon to a very clear declaration of true government policy, although it was not uttered by anyone with any apparent authority from the government on this occasion. The hon. member for Provencher suggested that it was absolutely unnecessary and unreasonable to expect that we should seek more than the answer of a minister or the people he proposed to bring forward. We have had plenty of evidence that we cannot rely on the statements of ministers. We have had plenty of evidence that they do not know what they are talking about when they make statements on behalf of their departments. We are not satisfied with statements of ministers here who one after another have made positive statements in regard to different problems within their
167G

Committee on Estimates departments and then within hours in one case and within days in other cases were proved to know nothing whatever about the subject they were discussing. We point out that if this were a standing committee, a perfectly normal procedure would be to call witnesses and to obtain evidence in regard to the facts.

speechtext:
Order. I have just refreshed my memory and I find that a motion was negatived yesterday. A motion was moved by Mr. Fulton, seconded by Mr. Blair, in these words:
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"and that the said committee have power to send for persons, papers and records."
In view of the fact that this motion was negatived by the house, I think the hon. Leader of the Opposition should refrain from references to that particular phase of this problem.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I shall not pursue it further. I regret that Your Honour did not notice that the hon. member for Provencher had been discussing that point at some considerable length.
On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I purposely did not discuss that point when the Speaker looked at me.
It is on the record.
Look at Hansard.
Hansard fortunately now speaks for itself.
Let it speak for itself.
Don't change it.

If the government really has any serious thought of making this committee on estimates an effective or an operative committee, and if there is one department that should be under examination, it is the Department of National Defence. That department, after all, directly or indirectly is responsible for the expenditure of nearly half of our very large budget. That department is one which certainly cannot be examined satisfactorily in the committee of the whole house.
Again I regret that it is necessary to deal with the speech of the hon. member for Provencher, because so little of it was relevant; but since it is the only statement made on behalf of the government I must take it that, up to this point at any rate, we should regard it as the explanation that is intended to come from the other side in regard to this motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister.
In his discussion of the subject he pointed out that there was a very different situation at Westminster, that there the estimates are so

involved that they would not be able to consider them in detail. Nevertheless he suggested that here there is, of course, ample opportunity to deal with them in the committee of the whole house. Well, there is not a thoughtful hon. member of this house who does not know perfectly well that it is impractical in the committee of the whole house to deal with the estimates of the Department of National Defence and, for that matter, with any other department, in the way they should be dealt wtih and could be dealt with. Why was it that in setting up standing committees there was the power granted to those committees, as a matter of right, to call witnesses and to call for the production of papers and documents?

speechtext: Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition has forgotten that I just drew to his attention the fact that discussion of that particular phase of this matter is out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I would point out once again that I was dealing with what was said by the hon. member for Provencher, and I was dealing with it in order to correct a misstatement which was made and which was permitted without any interjection from Your Honour when it was made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was not in the house when the words to which the hon. member has referred were spoken. I am now charged with the duty of trying to keep this debate relevant and in order. I have drawn to the attention of the Leader of the Opposition the fact that this very question was negatived yesterday. Under those circumstances I can do nothing else but ask him to refrain from referring to that phase of this problem.

I would point out that the 1947 committee on procedure recommended that we adopt in this house the same procedure in regard to all our committees that has been adopted at Westminster. That report of a committee of this house still stands as a matter of record. That report of a committee of this house, which after all represented the decision of members supporting this government as well as other members of this house, recommended a course which would have resulted automatically in our right to suggest the departments that should be examined. But even without that recommendation I submit that if this government really has any serious intention of making this committee operate, if this government is not merely making a pious pretence in its profession of offering some opportunity to examine the estimates, then it would name automatically, and even without request, the Department of National Defence.

Let any hon. members who are uncertain about how far the committees go in Westminster, which was suggested as the model by a committee on which the majority were members supporting this government, study the situation there. They will find that there the opposition is permitted to make suggestions as to the departments that should be called. There the opposition is given an opportunity to obtain information in regard to important subjects. If hon. member will read Hansard reports of the proceedings at Westminister they will find there the most detailed examination of the estimates' of the department of defence in the government of the United Kingdom. They will find that members of that committee travelled to different parts of the United Kingdom and called at various military installations, where there were brought before them not only senior officers but officials. They had senior members of the general staff before their committee, and they asked them questions. The most detailed information was given.
Is it to be suggested that here in Canada we are in a less favourable position to place under examination our staff officers and our officials dealing with defence activities than they are in Britain? In this country our defence activities are extremely important and call for the allocation of nearly half of our very large budget. Nevertheless not one hon. member in this house would suggest that there are as secret problems involved in our own case, nor would they suggest that the scope and the general scale of the responsibilities of our department of defence are commensurate with those of the department of defence in London.
They are able to come before a committee. They are able to give information. Upon the basis of that examination-granted only an examination in this case of a single department at one time-they are able to place before the house detailed recommendations which have resulted in substantial reform, not only in the matter of administration but in the matter of accounting methods as well.
We are suggesting nothing that is unusual. We are suggesting the practice we have adopted in regard to all our standing committees. We are suggesting a practice that has worked favourably in that jurisdiction that was recommended as our model for a committee of this house in 1947. May I once again emphasize that what we are asking is reasonable. What we are asking is consistent with our own practice. What we are asking is consistent with the practice that has been adopted elsewhere under a jurisdiction which follows our own parliamentary traditions.
Committee on Estimates
One thing that is certain-and I repeat it because it is in reference to the only statement that has been made on behalf of the government, or rather, I should say, on' behalf of the government from the government side of the house in regard to any of the details- is that parliament has not been asked to choose the departments. Parliament is not being permitted to choose the departments. If the hon. member for Provencher really believed, as he implied, that parliament should have that authority, then let him vote for this amendment and let the hon. members opposite vote for this amendment. Then he would be consistent for the first time.
However, this resolution-an important resolution, one sufficiently important that the government feels that it should be considered as only in its experimental stages-stands in the name of the Prime Minister, and we are waiting to hear from the Prime Minister any valid reason why this reasonable request should not be granted.

I desire at this time to say a few words concerning the proposed amendment, which expresses dissatisfaction with the setting up of the committee as it is presently proposed. First of all, I think all parties in the house agree that the committee is desirable. I know that over the years I have had the pleasure of being here it has been recommended and urged by members in various quarters of the house. Therefore I think it is desirable. I believe the public have a right to expect that the closest possible scrutiny will be given to the expenditures that are made here. Our expenditures are now approximately $5 billion, and from the correspondence I get and my contacts at home in my own riding I know that the people are concerned that the very closest examination be given the money that is expended here. I think the committee is welcomed by the members, and despite what the Leader of the Opposition has just said I think it is a fair statement to say that those who were members of the committee last year were well satisfied with the results.
I should like to take a moment to put on record the words of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) who, I might say, made a very worth-while contribution to the deliberations of the committee last year. I refer to the proceedings of the committee on estimates for Friday, March 18, 1955, and at page 427 I find that the hon. member for St. Paul's had this to say:
I should also like to put myself and my associates on record in expressing our appreciation of the assistance which has been given to this committee . . .
1G78	HOUSE OF
Committee on Estimates
The important thing is that these remarks were made on the last day of our consideration of the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, which all of us will remember was the most controversial so far as discussion was concerned. Then, the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Yuill) had this to say:
I would like to add my word of congratulation and commendation to the officials for the straightforward way in which they gave their answers to some of these problems. I think they have done a splendid job and I really feel that this committee is worth while . . .
I think it is fair to say that the chairman of the committee summed up the attitude of the members when he made these remarks:
It is very heart-warming to all concerned to think that when this important work of examining the estimates of a department of government on behalf of the people of Canada is over, that in spite of the differences we have had everybody can feel that the work has been well worth doing . . .
I have also taken the trouble to re-examine the work of the committee last year. It is now proposed that the committee be set up again and at present we have an amendment to the motion before us. I think the committee could be more useful, but I believe it can only become more useful with a change of attitude on the part of the official opposition. I say this in all seriousness. It is my understanding, and I believe the understanding of almost every member in the house regardless of party affiliation, that the committee should be used to get at the facts and examine the expenditures of the various departments under review, and that it should not be used as a forum for airing and re-airing a debate that has already taken place in this chamber.
I think the official opposition can be criticized on that point. Hon. members will recall that there were 36 sittings last spring, and I have taken the trouble to examine them. Of the 36 sittings, 16 were devoted to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. In other words over 40 per cent of the time taken by the committee was devoted ;o one department. In the estimates of the four departments examined there was an expenditure of $347 million involved; yet 40 per cent of the time of the committee was spent in examining 10 per cent of the estimates, so far as amount is concerned, that came before us.
As hon. members will recall, most of the time was spent in attempts on the part of the official opposition members of the committee to bring before the committee and rehash the report or working papers-I forget the description-of the subcommittee of the civil


liberties section of the Canadian Bar Association. Sixteen of the 36 sittings of the committee were spent on that department.
In my opinion the opposition have it within their power to make the committee more workable so that it will do a better job for the country generally. When the Leader of the Opposition is naming members of his party to that committee I suggest that he might well take a look behind him rather than beside him and put on the committee some of the backbenchers in his party, those to whom in our case he refers as following blindly. Incidentally, I do not see much division over there when it comes time to vote. He might give consideration to others than the ones who are involved in leadership over there, although perhaps "leadership" is too strong a word. I want to be fair. I think he might well consider some of those members who are elected to represent his party because of their ability as businessmen and responsible citizens in their own ridings. I am sure that in that party, as in all parties, there are many men who are capable of doing a job on the committee and are anxious to do so. I think he should give that some consideration. Let us forget political significance as far as this committee is concerned.
I am sure this is relevant to the motion.

I have often heard it said what a worth-while job is done by the committee on external affairs. For several years now the estimates of the department have been examined by that committee. I think it is a reasonable conclusion that the reason the committee has done useful work is that there has been a degree of unanimity as far as policy is concerned. The members of that committee have taken part in the work of the committee with a genuine desire to examine the estimates.
I think that can be done, and I would urge that more businessmen be given the opportunity to be members of this committee so as to get on with the job. I believe that suggestion will commend itself favourably to the majority of the fair-minded people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks in support of the resolution and the amendment. Both remind me very strongly of the situation Samson found himself in when his locks were shorn. He had a great name for power and strength, yet he found himself with neither strength nor a mind of his own. I feel that we have somewhat the same situation here. The committee has a powerful sounding name and is going to do wonderful

things but its teeth have been removed, particularly when the power to call for papers and witnesses is not granted.
I am not going to go any further on that.
I would criticize the resolution very mildly, and I should like to make what I hope will be suggestions to improve committees of this type as far as the present and future sessions are concerned. Many of us who are just rank and file members of this committee have for a long time felt frustrated and that we were wasting time because the items came before the committee and went away in the same condition exactly, intact as the government first presented them. We had made very little impact on them beyond, as someone said, the fact that we obtained a great deal of information and we had questions asked and answered. But we got no action as a result of those questions or that information. I have often heard good proposals made by the opposition scorned and turned down because they were not made from the government side.
It is that frustration which I feel is making our committees in general ineffective and almost useless. I would call the committees on which I have sat something much like what President Roosevelt used to call his evening fireside chat. That is about all the effectiveness we have. We are lulled into thinking we are doing something when actually we are only having a pleasant time, and we come back to the house and start the thing rolling again. It seems to me that under the present set-up of committees we are not even told to take it or leave it. We are told to take it. We do not get the chance of leaving it. We are obliged to take it. The government majority see to it that we do, and that is the result at the end of the sitting.
I realize that the government must keep certain control, but I cannot for the life of me see why in committees they should keep the same rigid, strong and overwhelming control they have in the house. I would suggest to them that we would get far more effective results from the committees if the government allowed their followers to have a free vote all through the working committees so the net result would be a consensus of opinion from those committees which would represent all parties.
Failing a free vote in all committees I would suggest, as has been done in Great Britain, that the government, in order to create a balance of fairness in that committee, should ask one of the opposition members to be chairman. I think it has been done in England very effectively and fairly. That takes away that strong bias, that strong tendency to railroad things through according to
Committee on Estimates government plan. It would indicate that the government are anxious to work with the opposition. I have seen good proposals made by the opposition, proposals which when made would carry the majority of the committee, but I have seen the vote withheld until the government side of the committee mustered some members in to vote with them. Those members came in.
I remember one instance two or three years ago. They knew nothing about the subject under discussion. They did not know the pros and cons of it. They did not know whether the resolution was a sound one, because they had not been there for the debate. Nevertheless they voted solidly, reminding one, as has often been said in this house, that they were a bunch of rubber stamps O.K.'ing what the government wanted on that particular item. This committee should have more power. True, it should not have power to pass laws, but it should have power to recommend something tangible to the house. I know that some recommendations have been made in the past, but they were very few and far between.
We are accused of being behind Great Britain by 40 years, but I suggest that we take steps to give more power to our committees, to change along the lines I have suggested. More than that, if the government wanted an effective committee and wanted an effective balance of views from the members in this house, I would suggest that every committee be composed of 50 per cent government supporters and 50 per cent opposition members. Failing that, I would suggest making the proportion 55-45. The present imbalance is not giving a true reflection of the thoughts of the people of this country while their members sit on the committee.
I am not going to say anything more about that matter, but I seriously make the suggestion that we are all anxious to see these committees functioning well, to the benefit of the people of this country. Until you get a better balance between the government group and the opposition group I am satisfied that you will never get effective action from any committee that is set up, no matter under what terms. More power must be given those committees to get the evidence required in order to come to conclusions.

Mr. Speaker, I am intervening again in the discussion on this resolution mainly because of the speech made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), a large part of which he devoted to what I think can correctly be described as a personal attack on myself and my participation in the work of the estimates committees last year.
1680	HOUSE OF
Committee on Estimates
However, I do not intervene solely for that reason, though I shall have something to say with reference to his charges. I intervene because, in addition, from two hon. members who have spoken from the government side we have heard words which make it abundantly clear, beyond any possibility of doubt that in the view of the members sitting opposite, committees of this sort will do effective, useful and acceptable work only so long as they come out with a unanimous report approving every action of the government and every proposal laid before them by way of estimates.
We have that view established out of the mouth of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland). He states his view of a good committee, namely the committee on external affairs. He said they believe-and I took down his words as accurately as I could- that committee does useful work because there is a large degree of unanimity.
On policy.
That is the criterion.
Unanimity on policy.

All right; I will accept that limitation. The criterion or the operative principle there must be borne in mind. What they dislike is opposition or questioning. Whether it be on policy or detail makes no difference. We have seen it too often, whether the criticism was with respect to policy or detail. That is when they begin to find the work of the committee unacceptable. It is almost a form of lese majesty; you are daring to criticize the views, the suggestions and proposals placed before you by this omnipotent, all-wise and always correct government.
That is their attitude. We saw it quite clearly mirrored in the statement of the hon. member and in the statement of the hon. member for Provencher. He said that the hon. member-referring to myself-criticized the work done by the committee last year and suggested that it could be improved. He said "If he found it annoying, I wish he would know just how annoying the other members on the committee found his efforts to criticize and to have changes made".
Mr. Speaker, I expected the hon. members of the Liberal party to be annoyed. I know that they are annoyed whenever any attempts are made to expose the fact that the proposals of the government are not sound; and particularly are they annoyed when attempts are made-as they are being made here today and as was done last night-to give the committee the power to make an impartial and independent inquiry into the government's proposals.


I find myself somewhat complimented and flattered by the words of the hon. member for Provencher. To listen to him you would think that, single-handed and alone, I had been able to frustrate the entire work of the committee, and that every other member of the committee was full of irritation over the motions I placed before that committee last year, and as we are now placing before the house this year, in an attempt to free the hands of the committee and make it possible for that committee to obtain independent evidence.
Let us look at the record, Mr. Speaker. I point out to you that last year, out of a total membership of 26, the Liberal party had 16 members, over two to one against the combined opposition. In the committee eight motions were made in an attempt to empower it, first of all, to call witnesses and call for papers. Then an attempt was made to have documents produced, something which was denied to us time after time. There were eight motions. Here is the record of the vote on those eight motions. The first motion was defeated by a vote of 7 to 11. I would ask you to bear in mind the fact that the proportionate membership of the committee was 16 Liberals out of a total of 26 or over two to one.
How do you get "two to one"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You are talking about quality, not quantity.
I am sorry; I should say over half the committee.
There is a slight difference. It is the usual distortion.

All right, then; over half the committee. The first vote was 7 to 11. Was that a situation where the Conservative members were alone in that vote? Here are the statistics which show that it was not a singlehanded effort, and it was only the opposition that was putting forward these suggestions. The second vote was 8 to 14. In each of these votes, except where I otherwise indicate, we were supported by members of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties on that committee. The third vote was 5 to 10; the fourth vote, 5 to 10; the fifth vote, 8 to 13; the sixth vote, 3 to 13, and that is the only vote in which Conservative party members voted alone against the government. The seventh vote was 4 to 7 and on that occasion only one Social Credit member supported us. The eighth was 8 to 14.
That is the record of what actually took place there. It should, of course, be pointed out that, as we know always happens in these cases, the government members present voted solidly to support the views of the minister,

who was not very backward in indicating the way he wanted them to vote.
But far from it being a single-handed attempt by one member, or even by one party, to expand the powers of this committee so we could get at the facts, the record of these votes clearly shows that in every case but one it was the combined vote of at least two and in most cases the three opposition parties. In each of the votes except one the proportion voting for the motion which we offered was higher than the proportion of the total combined membership of the opposition on that committee. That is the record, sir, and I think it is important that the house should bear in mind that there was a high proportion of the members of the committee last year who felt that efforts such as we are making now in the house to enlarge the scope and powers of this committee should be supported.
Coming then to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) now before us, let me point out that this suggests the committee itself should decide exactly what items of the estimates it will take up. This is in accordance with the practice that has prevailed in the United Kingdom parliament since the inception of their committee in 1912. When Mr. Speaker himself was in the chair at the time the hon. member for Eglinton presented this motion, as I recall it he asked for the authority upon which the hon. member said this was similar to the practice at Westminster. Although I believe that the motion presented at Westminster does vary in some slight particulars from the motion on the basis of which the committee was first set up, in principle it does not vary. Here is the motion introduced by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, as recorded at page 360 of Hansard of the United Kingdom parliament for 1912:
That a select committee be appointed to examine and report on such of the estimates presented to this house as may seem fit to the committee.
The motion of the hon. member for Eglin-ton is, of course, entirely in accordance with the practice prevailing over there.
What is necessary, sir, to make the work of this committee useful, to make the work of this committee contribute to a detailed and impartial scrutiny of the estimates presented by the government is not a change of attitude on the part of the members of the official opposition, as suggested by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland). What is necessary is that the government should be willing to release the fetters which it seeks now to place upon this committee. If these fetters are permitted to remain, as we saw very clearly last year when the committee got to work, 67509-107
Committee on Estimates they will be squeezed even tighter and tighter to further hamper the work of the committee.
So far as the statements by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) and other hon. members are concerned, which have been read, their effect is that we had before us senior civil servants. They were courteous, yes. They answered questions, yes. All those things were done, but we were not able to get other witnesses whom we wished to have before the committee. So far as those who did come were concerned, and so far as the questions which were put to them were concerned, they answered them in a courteous, friendly and helpful manner. The compliment paid by the hon. member for St. Paul's goes no further than that. To take that and try to say the hon. member for St. Paul's was saying we felt the committee was working in the way it should work is, of course, typical of the way in which my hon. friends opposite have to distort remarks out of their context and meaning in order to bolster their own very weak case.
I invite hon. members opposite to accept their responsibilities as members of parliament, to take an impartial approach and not reject the opportunity of determining themselves exactly what departments or what segments of departments they wish to investigate. If that is to be done, then this motion should be supported so the committee will have some independence of action.
If the motion is not supported by hon. members opposite, what are we to conclude? We are to conclude that they have no freedom of choice; that they have no opinion, no personal preference, no thoughts other than those suggested to them by the government as to which department they desire to investigate and how they wish to conduct the inquiry. They would be refusing to support a motion today, as they refused last night, which would give the committee the power, and that is all that is asked, to conduct its inquiry in the way it wanted. Instead of that, they will say, "No, we do not want to take even that power; we would prefer to conduct the inquiry exactly along the lines which our masters, the government, submit to us."
I urge my colleagues, even those who support the government, to remember that they will always have a majority on the committee. I take it that it is too much to hope that that situation would ever be changed.
