Mr. Speaker, I rise for but one purpose, namely to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in whose name this motion appears, to explain why the committee is to be circumscribed by having submitted to it only those departments that have been hand-chosen by the government. I do not know why the Prime Minister has not said something. Lately he has been on a number of sit-down strikes in regard to these matters of such great importance to the country.

If the motion is sufficiently important to merit its introduction by the Prime Minister, surely the house and the country are entitled to know from the Prime Minister, rather than from lesser members on the government side of the house, why so reasonable a request on the part of the opposition is being denied. When one reads the letter of the Prime Minister to the Leader of the Opposition it is a strange thing to find the Prime Minister saying that certain departments have been chosen, the Department of National Revenue, the Department of Labour, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Post Office Department, and that suitable arrangements have been made.
They have made suitable arrangements to appear before the committee. I do not know what these words "suitable arrangements" mean, but it is passing strange to me that departments should be warned months in advance that they are to be investigated, so they can make the necessary arrangements to give evidence before the committee.
What are those necessary arrangements, Mr. Speaker? It looks very much as if parliament is to have a peek into certain matters after those departments have made suitable arrangements to permit us to do so. As I see it, that is not the kind of investigation that was envisaged by the setting up of this committee, unless it is to be a kangaroo committee.
It will be.

No; I prefer to believe that it ought not to be. Surely the Prime Minister can explain why. Is the committee to be blindfolded? It is not allowed to see documents; it is to be denied witnesses, except those chosen by the government. Finally, it is to be restricted to those departments which have made the necessary suitable arrangements. Surely a committee set up in that way will return the kind of report that the government expects suitable arrangements will demand on the part of that committee.
A directed verdict.

I have no argument
about some of the departments of government that are to be submitted, but why not the Department of National Defence? That is the spending department today; that is the department that more than anything else over and over again is used as the basis for high taxation. The argument is used that taxation is high because of defence costs. Why is the Department of National Defence not included? It is not for me to say whether or not a military authority holding a high position was right when he said recently that

$120 million or more had been poured down the drain in connection with the production of certain aircraft already obsolete and out of date. Surely there was something to be investigated.
I cannot understand why this committee is to be confined to the departments the government chooses as those worthy of being investigated. The committee is to be a watchdog over the estimates, but it is to be muzzled in regard to that department in which the greatest expenditures take place. It is to be muzzled and blindfolded because it cannot call witnesses or see documents. It is to have brought before it such witnesses as the minister of the department, or the government in its wisdom, feels are proper to give evidence before it.
What kind of a verdict will be handed down by a court when one of the parties before that court picks out those witnesses who are to be heard, or if the judge just wants to hear one side, or the evidence of such witnesses as he desires to hear? What kind of a verdict would be rendered by a court of that kind? What kind of an independent verdict will be rendered by a court, the majority of whose members are appointed by and are responsible to the government? What are we trying to do? Is this to be just a caricature of a committee?
What possible objection can there be to allowing the committee to choose the departments it might look into and consider? Surely the government has not arrived at the point where it is afraid that its majority on the committee might choose departments other than those which the government desires? I do not think the government has much to fear in that regard. Again, I ask, what is this committee going to do? Is it going to be effective? The one in Great Britain is. Committee on Estimates coming before the committee to be considered after it has made the necessary suitable arrangements.

-I
want to add my own personal request that before the debate is over he make some contribution. No matter how limited, no matter how erroneous it may be in my opinion, I plead with him to make some contribution in the age-old tradition of decent, responsible government.
The amendment before us suggests that the committee should be permitted to select the departments it will consider. At the present time, under the motion as originally put forward and as further evidenced in the debate this afternoon, the government selects the departments that are to be examined by the committee. It flashes the red light to them a long time before and says in effect: Boys, get ready; the estimates committee is going to have a look at you. It will not be a very good look. We as a government will see to that by hedging them around with restrictions, by loading the committee with our members and by seeing that nothing that will bring about a really deep investigation goes through the house. We are going to do our best to protect you, but you never can tell about those opposition people who are on the committee. They work hard, they dig pretty deep, and even with all the stumbling blocks we put in their way it is quite possible that if you are not adequately prepared they might find out your misdeeds or misdoings.
Therefore the government say to their selected departments: Get ready for the committee. Smooth anything that you think might be embarrassing to yourselves. Prepare figures and make sure that the only figures you prepare are ones that will not be embarrassing to anybody. In effect the government say: We will be very annoyed if you go to the estimates committee and find yourselves caught off base, and that is why we are giving you all this notice. In effect that is the intent, purpose and actual operation under the present system.
Imagine the additional effectiveness of the committee if it made its own decision following its formation and within the matter of a few days called before it a given department and began to ask the minister of the department and, through him, the officials, questions as to its operation. How is it that defalcations in banks, for example, are discovered? As has been the case from time immemorial, they are discovered when the bank examiners walk in unexpectedly and say, "Let us have a look at your books and your operations".

think there is a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

No.
They are talking in their sleep.
You are looking for one.

How
is it that in businesses weaknesses, inaccuracies and defalcations are found? They are found when the auditors come in, sit down and examine the operations of the particular business. For a good many years it was my privilege to be one of the businessmen about whom the hon. member for Nipissing was talking. I want him to know that never in my experience did the auditors telephone me or my organization a week, a month or three months before and say, "We are going to come in and examine your books and records, so will you please make suitable arrangements."
I do know that on occasion in small ways- fortunately there have never been any big ones

the element of surprise has demonstrated its advantages in my ordinary business experience. For instance, let us take the case of petty cash from which someone had temporarily borrowed a few dollars to tide them over to pay day and had put in an I.O.U. That is the sort of thing which if you knew what was going to happen beforehand you would cover up by putting the money back in the box today instead of on pay day. However, the auditors walk in unexpectedly, and I have had them come to me and say that there was an I.O.U. in the petty cash from someone on the staff and ask me if I knew that this was taking place and whether I had authorized it.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that some of these business illustrations are difficult for the professional politicians on the government side to comprehend, but I put them forward because I know they are easily understandable to the businessmen in this section of the house. I believe definitely that the element of surprise is lost by warning departments in advance, preselecting them several months before and then having their operations rubber stamped by the government majority. The principle of warning departments in this way is not a fundamentally sound idea. It detracts from the usefulness, vitality and ability of the committee to seek out information.
Another point in that connection which might well be made arises from the reference in the Prime Minister's letter, to the departments making suitable arrangements. To me
Committee on Estimates that indicates a lack of confidence on the part of the Prime Minister and the cabinet in the civil service and the departments under their direction. If I should ever occupy a seat on the treasury benches, where I would listen to the catcalls from this point, it would be my hope to have the kind of department that people could come and look at at any time, a department that would not have to have advance warning. If you have to have advance warning it indicates that something is wrong. It indicates that it is necessary to sweep the dirt under the carpet.
In this connection the last question which I would leave hanging in the air is simply this. What is the government hiding that they have to follow this particular course of action? Why will they not face up to an unfettered committee free to follow where its instinct and intelligence lead? The Prime Minister is still in the house, Mr. Speaker. I am sure he might have something to say on this subject. I hope that he will in some way express his opinion on his own motion. I do not think he would want to bring into this world a baby that was completely fatherless. That seems to be the way it stands at the present time.

Just before I put the question, for the information of the hon. member for Eglinton and the house, may I indicate why I said earlier that I had some doubts as to the amendment being in order. I may say immediately that I will allow the amendment. I will allow it, not because I am not sure of my ground but because I believe that the point is a rather difficult one and one upon which I think it is appropriate that I should only enter a caveat before I allow the amendment.
The two grounds are as follows. The first is that whereas the motion which is on the order paper merely proposes to set up a committee without giving the order of reference, the amendment is a major alteration to the notice of motion and proposes what the order of reference will be. According to Beauchesne, third edition, citation 315:
A new notice must be given in the Votes and Proceedings, under standing order 45,-
Now standing order 41.
-when a material change is to be made to a notice of motion before it is taken up by the house.
The second point has to do with the difference between the wording of the amendment or the motion as amended, and the wording which is supposed to have been copied from the United Kingdom order of

Committee on Estimates reference for the formation of such a committee. I was lucky enough to obtain, through the good offices of the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Kamloops, the book which was referred to earlier in the debate by both hon. members. It is entitled "Parliamentary Debates, 5th Series, volume 37, 1912". The Chancellor of the Exchequer, who was then Mr. Lloyd George, in bringing in his motion, moved it in the following terms:
That a select committee be appointed to examine and report on such of the estimates presented to this house as may seem fit to the committee.
The question that I should like hon. members to ponder is this, and it is the reason I am not making a ruling. I have in my hand treasury paper No. 6 of the United Kingdom which is entitled "Parliamentary Supply Procedure" and was issued by the treasury for official use in January, 1949. At page 58 I find the following:
For present purposes the important part of this report-
An earlier part of the report recommended that the house continue having a committee on estimates.
-is that in which the committee reaffirmed the desirability that the estimates should be examined by a select committee, in addition to and if possible prior to, their consideration in committee of supply.
In the United Kingdom I believe they do not withdraw from the committee of supply the estimates that are to be considered by the committee on estimates.
Nor do we.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Here our practice has been different. As to the estimates pertaining to government-owned railways, to the Department of External Affairs, or to the departments referred to the committee on estimates last year, it had been the practice to move that these estimates be removed from the committee of supply and referred to the committee on estimates and then, when they are reported back by the committee, there had to be another motion to send them back to the committee of supply.
1 ask hon. members who made that motion to get them from there where they are now and who made that motion to bring them back? That is government business, and must be moved by the leader of the house. If the house wish to accept this motion, as the wording is now it would read as follows:
That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may seem fit to the committee and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.
Unless the house were assured that there would be made by the leader of the house a

motion to extract some estimates from the committee of supply, saving all the power of that committee to consider them later, and that when they were reported by the committee a motion would be made by the leader of the house to send them back here, it would be absolutely inoperative. That was the procedure until it was altered by standing order 57.
As I said before, I am not going to make a ruling because I am not too sure about the practice of the United Kingdom, and I do not want to deal any further with it because I think in doing so I would be debating a question which has been at issue between the two sides in the house.

Committee on Estimates

I find on page 2 of the estimates not only 19 major departments, but also a good many minor departments which will still have to be dealt with by the committee of the whole.
This afternoon the hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested that he felt it was the duty of parliament to examine the estimates. I could not agree with anything more. Should not some parliamentary committee look into the way in which that money is being spent? I think for a moment of the Bank of Canada. After all, the Bank of Canada directs Canadian financial policy. Surely it is sensible for some parliamentary committee to look into its activities. I think of Eldorado Mining and Refining Company, a company which has so much to do with the production of uranium for the free world. Surely it is sensible for a parliamentary committee to examine the way in which that company is spending its money.
I could mention crown assets; I could mention the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, a company which plays such a role in encouraging Canada's export trade. I say that every crown corporation owned by the people of Canada should be brought before one parliamentary committee or another at least once a year. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard):
That the motion be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:
"and that the estimates of any department or crown corporation, not already referred to a standing or select committee, be referred forthwith to such a committee for examination and report."
I say, Mr. Speaker, if the house would pass this particular motion, in future if there is waste and extravagance in some of these departments or corporations, parliament would have a much better chance of finding it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have listened very carefully to the terms of the hon. member's amendment 

and I regret to have to inform him that I cannot accept it. Citation 315 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, reads as follows:
A modification of a notice of motion standing upon the notice paper is permitted, if the amended notice does not exceed the scope of the original notice.
A new notice must be given in the Votes and Proceedings, under standing order 45, when a material change is to be made to a notice of motion before it is taken up by the house.
I would also refer the hon. member to certain rulings which have been made on this subject. I have one in mind particularly, where the house was considering the setting up of a committee for the purpose of considering the accounts of a government-owned railway. An amendment had been moved to empower the committee to also consider the accounts of a private company. This was ruled out of order by Mr. Speaker Black at page 642 of Beauchesne's third edition. Mr. Guthrie raised a point of order and said it is a substantive motion and should be brought before the house as such with notice given in the ordinary way. Mr. Speaker Black declared the point of order well taken.
There are other rulings in Beauchesne to which I could refer the hon. member. One appears at page 633 and is the ruling of Mr. Speaker Lemieux. Another one appears at page 635, a ruling of Mr. Deputy Speaker Fred Johnston. I am sorry, but I cannot accept the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not going to challenge your ruling. As a matter of fact I rather expected it. However, in view of the latitude you showed when the last motion was moved I was rather hoping you might let me proceed. As I say, however, I am not going to hold up the house at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief and will endeavour to be finished before six o'clock. I have two or three observations to make, the first one being that the hon. member for Eglinton complained that we delayed the placing of this motion before the house. Surely it is obvious to the house, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation which should have been disposed of first this session was that on which an engagement had been made to introduce that legislation in the house.
When we met here we were under the criticism of previous years that we had interrupted the address debate, and because of the new rules we were asked to continue the debate

until it was concluded. We did that. We then took up the legislation, as I say, on which I had given an engagement to the banks; and it we had not done that I am satisfied that hon. members of the Conservative party would have claimed we were ignoring parliament and not submitting to the judgment of parliament that decision of last November.
I want to refer very briefly to what the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre has said about all estimates going to committees. I realize that he is away ahead of many hon. members of the house, but perhaps that is consistent with the attitude he has taken throughout. I might also say he is apparently consistent in trying to save money in the speeches he makes in this house. It was suggested to me by one of my colleagues last night that it would be interesting if we sent to some committee all the suggestions made by opposition members for the spending of money, to have a price tag put on them.
Last night the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made a remark which I think we ought to examine not now but at some future time. His suggestion, I think, was that we should continue to send before this committee members of the civil service, of whatever rank they may be, ultimately to find someone who would disagree with government policy. Now it is my-

speechtext:
Yes. And, Mr. Speaker, he went on to say that he wants to find out whose idea a particular thing was. The whole essence of parliamentary government is that the civil servants will carry out the orders of parliament and government policy. Whether or not they agree with it in the first instance they are of course obliged to give their opinion, and once an opinion is given and once a policy is announced it is their duty to carry it out.
I have just one more point, and it has to do with the remarks made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition with respect to the business of this committee. I have always said that this was an experiment, and I took some pains during my address a year
Committee on Estimates ago to point out the difference between what we thought an estimates committee should be-and when I say "we" I mean parliament and all parties in it, not the government-as compared to that of the United Kingdom. I made the point that we did not expect, and I had never heard anyone in this house suggest, that we would end up with an estimates committee such as they have in the United Kingdom.
In the United Kingdom the committee of supply deals with policy and the committee on estimates deals with detail. Thus far we have not come to a conclusion here as to whether or not the estimates committee should deal with policy or detail. Nevertheless we never did expect-at least I do not think anyone expected-that we would have a committee which would travel throughout Canada, take evidence from sundry people, and publish a report months after the estimates were placed before parliament. The whole purpose of the estimates committee is to deal during the current session with the estimates that are submitted, so that parliament may be entitled to reject them if it feels it advisable during that session.
I have nothing further to add except that with respect to the work of the committee we did as the Prime Minister indicated we would do in the letter he wrote in response to the letter written by the Leader of the Opposition. In this letter the Prime Minister indicated that we had decided to recommend to parliament that four departments come before the committee. It should be noted, however, that in reading that particular portion of my address the Leader of the Opposition did not go on to read the following paragraph in which I said that having done that, and having in mind the amount of time parliament would have, we would do our best to meet the wishes of the opposition and call some other departments if we had time.
Motion (Mr. St. Laurent, Quebec East) agreed to.
